# US Dictionary

> > A comprehensive resource for American English idioms, phrases, and expressions with detailed etymologies and historical origins.

US Dictionary explores the meanings, definitions, and historical origins of idioms and conversational phrases used in American English. Each entry traces phrases back to literary sources including Shakespeare, Dickens, Hemingway, and classical works, providing context for modern usage in everyday communication.

## Key Topics

- idiom definitions
- phrase origins
- etymology
- American English expressions
- conversational English
- figurative language
- William Shakespeare
- Old English
- literary references
- phrase meanings
- communication phrases
- English idioms
- historical linguistics
- classical literature influences

## Common Conversational Phrases

- [How's It Going: Definition, Meaning and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/hows-it-going): Casual greeting phrase origin and conversational usage in US English
- [What's Going On: Definition, Meaning and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/whats-going-on): Common phrase etymology featuring Marvin Gaye song and historical usage
- [I Hear You: Definition, Meaning and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/i-hear-you): Empathy phrase from Killigrew with active listening communication tips
- [How About You: Definition, Meaning and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/how-about-you): Conversational English phrase with Payne Fund Studies references
- [Thanks for Checking Up on Me: Definition, Meaning, How to Reply](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/thanks-for-checking-up-on-me): Gratitude expression guide with Hemingway references and reply examples
- [Keeping in Touch: Definition, Meaning, and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/keeping-in-touch): Communication phrase history from The Magazine of Business era

## Emotional and Psychological Expressions

- [Get Over It: Definition, Meaning, and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/get-over-it): Emotional recovery phrase from Memoirs of Serjeant Paul Swanston
- [Mind Over Matter: Definition, Meaning and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/mind-over-matter): Willpower phrase from Virgil, Plato, and Sir Charles Lyell's works
- [Be Still My Heart: Definition, Meaning and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/be-still-my-heart): Romantic expression from Homer's Odyssey through Dryden and Pope
- [Oh My Gosh: Definition, Meaning and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/oh-my-gosh): Surprise exclamation euphemism from Augusta J. Evans' St. Elmo

## Social and Cultural Idioms

- [Here's To You: Definition, Meaning And Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/heres-to-you): Toasting phrase history tracing back to Greeks and Romans traditions
- [All The Best To You: Definition, Meaning And Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/all-the-best-to-you): Well-wishing farewell phrase with Congressional Record references
- [Bougee: Definition, Meaning, and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/bougee): Modern slang term for bourgeois lifestyle and social class references
- [Chillin: Definition, Meaning and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/chillin): Youth slang from Xscape's 'Just Kickin' It' and US informal language
- [Get With Someone: Definition, Meaning and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/get-with-someone): Dating slang from Dark Shadows and modern relationship terminology

## Classical and Literary Idioms

- [Ebb and Flow: Definition, Meaning, and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/ebb-and-flow): Idiom definition exploring Shakespeare's 'ebb and flow' from Old English
- [A Cog in the Wheel: Definition, Meaning and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/a-cog-in-the-wheel): Workplace idiom from University of New York Annual Report references
- [Trick Him Into: Definition, Meaning, and Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/trick-him-into): Deception idiom from Dickens' Bleak House and Old North French roots
- [Tuesday's Child Is Full Of Grace: Definition, Meaning And Origin](https://usdictionary.com/idioms/tuesdays-child-is-full-of-grace): Nursery rhyme folklore from A.E. Bray's Traditions of Devonshire
